scopeReview: PSO-4.B.1–2: sovereignty, nation-states and self-determination; colonialism/imperialism, independence and devolution along national lines shaping boundaries. Ghana independence and Scottish devolution provide verified contrasting examples. No contested recognition or automatic secession claim.
varietyReview: Institutional chronology, inherited-boundary settlement map, policy-field transfer chart and consultation table. Other cases distinguish direct rule from connections, choice from predetermined outcome, overlapping claims, internal authority and interdependence. Four meaningful stimuli and all five skills.
repetitionReview: Process-oriented evidence distinguishes this set from4.1 entity classification. Numeric items address authority allocation and voting denominators, not arbitrary arithmetic; boundary continuity is given by a historical premise rather than inferred from appearance. No exact duplicate or numeric-only clone.
referenceNote: Primary institutional accounts checked; all numerical/territorial cases are invented and clearly labeled. No actual referendum is predicted or legal entitlement adjudicated. Research references remain QA-only; existing approved resource collection unchanged. Automated verification is not human review or empirical calibration.

questions.correctOption: The 1960 transfer of external and domestic authority to independent K.
questions.independentReview: Checked the sequence and the explicit external-authority column. Only1960 removes colonial control and establishes K’s independence;1990 is internal devolution and does not duplicate the independence event.

questions.correctOption: A change in the line’s political status can divide an existing national distribution without moving its residents.
questions.independentReview: Verified R dots lie on both sides of x40 and the two polygons meet at that same inherited line. The supplied before/after status changes, while locations remain fixed; classification does not require unrecorded migration.

questions.correctOption: Three fields shift from central to regional administration, consistent with devolution rather than independence.
questions.independentReview: Recomputed4+6=10 and7+3=10; regional change+3,central−3. Distinct fields are counted once, and the caption does not equate field counts with comparable power or fiscal weight.

questions.correctOption: Autonomy receives 60% of valid votes, equal to 48% of registered voters.
questions.independentReview: Independently computed480+320=800,800/1000=.8,480/800=.6,480/1000=.48,320/1000=.32. All cast ballots are stipulated valid; registered voters are not silently equated with all residents or all citizens.

questions.correctOption: Decolonization through the establishment of an independent state.
questions.independentReview: Verified Gold Coast→Ghana1957 in the UN’s former non-self-governing-territory record and Ghana judiciary’s independence chronology. Avoided inaccurate claims that Ghana was the first independent African or sub-Saharan state.

questions.correctOption: Devolution of governing responsibilities within an existing state.
questions.independentReview: Checked the Scottish Parliament’s current powers explanation directly. The item does not predict future independence, treat all matters as devolved, or equate UK arrangements with every federal constitution.

questions.correctOption: An external power appoints the territory’s governor and directly controls its public administration.
questions.independentReview: Compared direct territorial administration with noncontrolling international connections. Did not define all foreign trade as imperialism or make large-scale settler migration a necessary condition of colonialism.

Checked the self-determination principle against the UN Charter context. The question identifies a geographic-political concept rather than adjudicating a legal right to secede or prescribing a binding referendum outcome.

questions.correctOption: National self-determination claims can overlap, so drawing a border may not satisfy every community’s territorial aims.
questions.independentReview: Reviewed competing territorial claims as a general political-geographic mechanism without selecting a winner or assigning identities from location. A border can change jurisdiction while leaving minority or overlapping claims unresolved.

questions.correctOption: A change establishing independent state authority, rather than only the specified internal transfer.
questions.independentReview: Checked the stated allocation rather than inferring sovereignty from symbols or spending. The question does not assume a uniform international recognition rule; it asks what distinguishes independence from internal governance.

questions.correctOption: An independent state can choose international cooperation without thereby ceasing to be a state.
questions.independentReview: Distinguished formal political status, interdependence and actual allocated powers. No particular treaty is interpreted; voluntary links alone cannot establish loss of all sovereignty or renewed direct colonial control.
